name: walkthrough
title: Scheme Essentials
description: Walk through the labeled Scheme examples in this tutorial, from the one syntax rule and lists through recursion, higher-order functions, let, association lists, and closures. Each step explains what the code does and what the REPL prints.

steps.description: Every compound form in Scheme is a parenthesized list with the operator first. Arithmetic is not special: `+`, `*`, `define`, and `if` all use the same shape.
The nesting sets the order. Scheme evaluates `(+ 2 3)` first, then multiplies that result by 4, so line 2 prints 20.
`define` binds the name `pi` to the number 3.14159. `if` tests `(> 5 0)` and returns its first branch, the string `"positive"`.
Move to lists. This block builds a list and shows the three operations that take one apart and put it back together.
`list` builds a list from its arguments, and `'` (quote) marks `a`, `b`, and `c` as symbols, names in their own right rather than names to look up. Line 1 binds the list to `L`.
`car` returns the first element, `cdr` returns everything after the first, and `cons` returns a new list with its first argument on the front of its second.
`null?` tests for the empty list and returns `#t`. `pair?` tests for a nonempty list and returns `#t` for `L`.
Move to functions. This block defines one function two ways and calls it.
`define` binds the name `square` to a `lambda` expression. The `lambda` takes one argument, `n`, and returns `(* n n)`.
Line 5 writes the same function in shorthand: `(define (square n) (* n n))` binds `square` to a function of `n`.
The call `(square 7)` multiplies 7 by 7 and returns 49.
Move to conditionals. This block writes the same choice with `if` and with `cond`.
`sign` uses `if`, which takes a test and exactly two branches. It returns `'negative` when `n` is below zero and `'non-negative` otherwise.
`classify` uses `cond`, which takes any number of test-and-result clauses. It checks `< 0`, then `= 0`, then `else`.
`map` calls `classify` once per element and collects the results into a list.
Move to functions as values. This block binds a name to the addition function itself.
`+` is a value, the addition function. Line 1 binds the name `add` to it, so `add` and `+` name the same function.
Calling `add` with 3 and 2 runs addition and returns 5.
Move to recursion. Scheme has no loop, so iteration is a function that calls itself on a shorter list.
`sumlist` recurses over a list. It checks `(null? (cdr L))` for the base case, returns the last element, and otherwise adds the first element to the sum of the rest.
The base case stops at the last element, not at the empty list.
`(sumlist (cdr L))` calls `sumlist` on the shorter list, so each call moves one step closer to the base case.
Move to a second recursion. `largest` finds the biggest element of a list.
`largest` returns the biggest element by recursion. The base case returns the last element, and the `if` compares the first element against the largest of the rest.
`(largest (cdr L))` appears in both the test and the else branch. Both calls compute the same value.
Move to the fixed version. This block names the subresult once with `let`.
`largest2` computes `(largest2 (cdr L))` once and binds it to `largestval` with `let`. The `if` then compares `(car L)` against `largestval`.
The `let` binding holds one value for the rest of the expression, so the recursive call runs once per level.
Move to a walk that stops early. `contains?` searches a list and returns as soon as it finds a match.
`contains?` walks a list looking for `x`. It returns `#f` for the empty list, `#t` when the first element matches, and otherwise recurs on the rest.
The recursive call sits in tail position: nothing runs after it returns, so Scheme can run it without growing the stack.
`(null? l)` is the base case. It returns `#f`, because an empty list holds no matching element.
Move to higher-order functions. This block passes functions to `map` and `apply`.
`L1` and `L2` hold two lists of numbers.

`map` takes a function as its first argument and applies it element by element. With two lists it pairs them up, so `-` subtracts each pair. `apply` spreads a list into a function's arguments, so `(apply + '(1 2 3))` is `(+ 1 2 3)`.
Line 5 passes a `lambda` to `map` to square each element. Line 6 applies a `lambda` on the spot by putting it in the operator position.
Move to an anonymous function applied immediately. This block creates a function inside another and calls it right away.
`plusminus` has two functions. The outer one is named; the inner one is a `lambda` that builds a list of the sum and difference of its two arguments.
The call `((lambda (x y) ...) a b)` puts a function expression in the operator position. Scheme creates the inner function, applies it to `a` and `b`, and discards it.
`plusminus` with 6 and 2 returns the list `(8 4)`, the sum and the difference.
Move to lifting the operator out. This block turns the summing function into one that takes its operator as a parameter.
`oplist` is `sumlist` with the operator lifted out to a parameter `op`. It combines the first element with the result of the rest using whatever `op` you pass.
Line 5 uses `op` in place of `+`, so the same function adds, multiplies, or does anything else.
Passing `*` multiplies, passing `+` adds, and `apply` gives the same product as `oplist` with `*`.
Move to `let`. This block names a value once and uses it twice.
`let` binds a name for one expression. Line 1 computes `(+ 2 3)` once and binds it to `x`; line 2 multiplies `x` by itself.
`(x (+ 2 3))` is one binding pair. The extra parentheses around it make a list holding that pair, and `let` wraps that list around the body.
Move to a `let` with two bindings. This block binds two names in the same expression.
A `let` can bind more than one name. This one binds `a` to 3 and `b` to 4, then adds their squares.
Each binding is one pair, and the pairs sit together in a list. Scheme computes both values from the outside environment.
Move to association lists. This block builds a small lookup table out of pairs.
`ops` is an association list, or alist: a list of pairs that maps each key to a value. `cons` builds each pair.
The keys are the symbols `'+` and `'-`; the values are the functions `+` and `-`. The page looks up a key in this list with `assq`.
Move back to `apply`, this time with a list of numbers.
`apply` takes a function and a list and spreads the list into separate arguments. Line 2 calls `+` directly with a list, which is an error because `+` wants numbers, not a list.
`(apply + '(1 2 3))` is the same call as `(+ 1 2 3)`.
Move to closures. This block returns a function that remembers a value between calls.
`make-counter` returns a closure: a function that captures the `count` binding from the `let`. Each call to the returned function adds 1 to `count` with `set!` and returns the new value.
The `let` creates one `count` per call to `make-counter`, and the `lambda` closes over that binding.
`counter1` and `counter2` come from two separate calls, so each holds its own `count`.

steps.question: Each `(counter1)` call adds 1 to its own count. What does the `(counter2)` call print?
